title: Single Mothers Are Getting Older
author: Anne Morse
summary: Morse, a demographer, takes a statistic that looks inert and shows that it conceals a substantial change. The nonmarital share of U.S. births has hovered near 40 percent for more than a decade, but the age composition of those births has shifted sharply, and in 2024 the birth rate to unmarried women aged 40 to 44 exceeded the birth rate to unmarried teenagers for the first time. She decomposes the trend: the overall unmarried birth rate for women 15 to 44 fell 19 percent between 2014 and 2024, driven overwhelmingly by a 47 percent collapse in the unmarried teen rate and declines of 31 and 17 percent among women in their early and late twenties. Meanwhile the rate for unmarried women over 35 rose 15 percent and the rate for those over 40 rose 40 percent. She also corrects a common misreading by noting that while most teen births are nonmarital, only 9 percent of nonmarital births are to teens, with 57 percent occurring to women in their twenties. The share of nonmarital births to women under 30 fell from 84 percent in 2000 to 66 percent in 2024. Her closing argument is interpretive rather than statistical: because unmarried motherhood is widely used as a proxy for economic disadvantage, a change in who the unmarried mothers are should change what the indicator is taken to mean.
points: The headline stability of the roughly 40 percent nonmarital birth share masks two offsetting movements, a steep decline among the young and a rise among women over 35.
Because there are far more unmarried teenage girls than unmarried women in their late thirties, the older group needed a much higher rate to surpass teen births in count, which it did in 2023.
Morse separates the teen-birth and nonmarital-birth questions: 92 percent of teen births are nonmarital, yet teens account for just 9 percent of nonmarital births.
The unmarried birth rate for women over 40 rose from 8.5 to 11.9 per 1,000 between 2014 and 2024, a 40 percent increase.
The analytic payoff is that a shifting age profile may change the social meaning and economic context of nonmarital childbearing, not just its distribution.
quotes: Marriage, childbearing, and economic security have become increasingly linked, making births outside of marriage a useful indicator for understanding inequality.

This initially seems like a remarkably stable statistic in an era marked by shifting birth and marriage rates. But beneath that stable statistic, a demographic transformation is underway. It passed a quiet milestone in 2024 when the birth rate to unmarried women ages 40 to 44 surpassed the birth rate to unmarried teenagers.
The birth rate to unmarried women, ages 15 to 44, declined by 19% in the decade between 2014 and 2024

The birth rate for unmarried teenagers declined by 47% between 2014 and 2024. The trend in the unmarried teen birth rate closely matches the overall teen birth rate, because the vast majority (92%) of births to teens occur outside of marriage.
In fact, only 9% of all births to unmarried women are to teenagers. By contrast, over half (57%) of all unmarried births occur to women in their 20s.
Notably, 2024 was the first year where the birth rate to unmarried women ages 40-44 was higher than the birth rate to unmarried teens.
In 2000, 84% of births to unmarried mothers were to women under 30. By 2024, this had decreased to 66 percent. In fact, over a third of all births to unmarried mothers today are to women over 30.

As the age profile of unmarried motherhood shifts, so too,may the social meaning, economic context, and consequences of unmarried childbearing, both for the women and children in question and for society.
